common_name: Gillian Blades Clematis (White Large-Flowered Clematis with Pale Mauve Stripe)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

directions: Gillian Blades bears large, ruffled, pure white flowers with a faint pale mauve central stripe on each tepal and prominent cream anthers, opening in late spring to early summer and again more sparsely in late summer on a Group 2 (early large-flowered) framework. Its ruffled, slightly twisted tepals give the flower a fuller, more textured look than many white clematis, and the plant has earned a long-standing reputation as a reliable, free-flowering garden performer. Prune lightly in late winter, removing only dead or weak growth above the lowest strong buds, since it flowers on both old and new wood.

common_name: Sylvia Denny Clematis (Double White Early Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

directions: Sylvia Denny opens fully double, pure white flowers with a faint green cast at the center on the previous year's ripened wood in late spring, then produces simpler single white flowers on new growth later in the season, giving two distinct looks from the same plant across one bloom period. This Group 2 (early large-flowered) habit means it should be pruned lightly in late winter, cutting back only to the topmost pair of strong, healthy buds rather than hard to the base, to preserve the old wood responsible for the earlier double flush.

common_name: John Warren Clematis (Giant Pale Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Deep Red Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

directions: Raised by English clematis breeder Barry Fretwell, John Warren produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, pale mauve-pink tepals with wavy, ruffled edges and a bold deep carmine-red central bar, often exceeding 8 inches across at their peak in early summer with a lighter repeat bloom in late summer. Its vigorous, sturdy growth needs a substantial support such as a large obelisk or arbor. Prune as a Group 2 (early large-flowered) type, removing only dead or weak stems back to a strong pair of buds in late winter to preserve the framework that carries the earliest, largest flowers.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

directions: Bred by Polish clematis hybridizer Szczepan Marczynski, Taiga opens as a dense, pompon-like double flower in unusual shades of lime-green, cream, and dusky purple that gradually separates into a starry outer layer of purple-pink tepals surrounding a green-and-cream double center as the bloom ages, giving each flower a changeable, multi-stage appearance through summer and into fall. As a Group 3 (late large-flowered) clematis, cut all stems back hard to a strong pair of buds about 12 inches above the ground in late winter to encourage the new growth that carries these unusual flowers.

common_name: Omoshiro Clematis (Blush Pink-and-White Bicolor Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

directions: Bred in Japan, Omoshiro, a name loosely translating to interesting or delightful, bears large, rounded white flowers heavily blushed with pink toward the tepal margins, with the pink deepening in cooler weather and fading toward white in summer heat, giving the display a changeable, two-toned character through the season. It flowers on both old and new wood, so it is generally pruned as a Group 2 (early large-flowered) type, removing only dead or weak stems back to a strong pair of buds in late winter.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown at soil level in lean, well-drained, limestone-based or neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this prairie species resents rich, moist, or heavy clay soil.

directions: Native to limestone prairies and glades of the central United States, notably Missouri, Kansas, and Nebraska, where it is a conservation concern in parts of its range, Fremont's leather flower produces thick, urn-shaped, leathery lavender-purple flowers with recurved, woolly-margined tips held upright on short stems from late spring into early summer, followed by fluffy silvery seed heads. It has no tendrils and forms a low, non-climbing clump rather than a vine, thriving on neglect in rock gardens, dry prairie plantings, and other lean, well-drained sites where richer soil or competition from taller plants causes it to decline. Leave the deep taproot undisturbed once established, since this species resents transplanting after its first year or two.

common_name: Pure Joy Sedum (White-Flowered Blue-Green SunSparkler Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring once soil is workable, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Pure Joy is a low, mounding SunSparkler-series selection with smooth blue-green foliage and clusters of pure white starry flowers in late summer, standing out among its mostly pink- and burgundy-flowered series-mates as one of the few white-blooming SunSparkler introductions. Its compact, wide-spreading habit suits the front of a border, rock garden, or container edge. Avoid rich or consistently moist soil, which encourages floppy growth and crown rot, and divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; closely related to Sedum kamtschaticum but with smoother, rounder, untoothed leaves.

directions: All-Gold Stonecrop forms a tidy, spreading mound of rounded, smooth-edged, bright green succulent leaves topped by dense, flat-topped clusters of bright golden-yellow starry flowers in summer, valued for edging, rock gardens, and small-scale groundcover where its neater, untoothed foliage distinguishes it from the more common, scalloped-leaved Sedum kamtschaticum. It tolerates poor, dry soil once established and needs little care beyond dividing congested clumps every few years in spring.

planting.note: Press rooted divisions or stem fragments into very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; native to rocky slopes of Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean.

directions: This Turkish native resents wet feet and heavy clay far more than it minds neglect or poor fertility. Tiny, densely packed, needle-like green leaves flush red-bronze under summer heat and drought stress, then carry small clusters of white starry flowers over the tight mat in early to midsummer. Its very low, dense habit makes it well suited to rock garden crevices, gravel paths, green roofs, and trough gardens where taller groundcovers would overwhelm neighboring alpine plants. Divide congested patches in spring to keep the mat vigorous.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; native to rocky outcrops of Western Europe including Wales and France.

directions: Rock Stonecrop forms tight rosette-tipped clusters of whorled, needle-like blue-green foliage on creeping, mat-forming stems, sending up flat-topped heads of bright yellow starry flowers on short stalks in early summer. Native to rocky, acidic outcrops in Wales and western France, it tolerates poor, dry, stony soil where richer plantings fail, making it useful for rock gardens, wall crevices, and gravel plantings. Remove spent flower stalks after bloom and divide crowded patches in spring to maintain a tight, tidy mat.

planting.note: Scatter seed or press rooted cuttings into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; short-lived but self-sows readily to maintain a persistent carpet.

directions: Spanish Stonecrop forms a fine-textured mat of slender, blue-gray, needle-like foliage that often blushes pink to lavender under stress from heat, cold, or drought, topped by small white-to-pale-pink starry flowers in early summer. Although individual rosettes are short-lived, behaving more as annuals or biennials, the species self-sows and spreads readily enough to maintain a persistent, ever-renewing carpet, which has made it a popular component of extensive green-roof plantings and gravel gardens across a very wide hardiness range. It needs essentially no supplemental water once established and tolerates poor, rocky soil that would stress most other groundcovers.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Coral Beads develops its deepest bronze-red color in bright light and stays greener in shade.

directions: Coral Beads is a trailing Mexican sedum densely strung with small, plump, bead-like leaves that shift from soft green to coppery bronze-red under bright, cool, dry conditions, forming a cascading mound well suited to hanging baskets and shallow succulent dishes. Its brittle stems shed leaves easily at a touch, a trait shared with many bead-leaved sedums, but each fallen leaf roots readily where it lands, making propagation effortless. Water only after the soil has dried completely, and protect from frost, since it is hardy only in essentially frost-free climates.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Popcorn Sedum blushes red at the leaf tips in bright light and stays plain glossy green in shade.

directions: Popcorn Sedum forms dense rosette clusters of plump, glossy, rounded bright green leaves on trailing-to-sprawling stems, with leaf tips blushing red to coral under bright light and drought stress; crushed foliage releases a distinctive sharp, resinous scent often compared to buttered popcorn. It branches and roots readily from stem or leaf cuttings, making it an easy, fast-growing choice for succulent arrangements and hanging containers. Water only when the soil is fully dry and protect from frost.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; native to rocky slopes of Afghanistan and the western Himalayas.

directions: Himalayan Stonecrop forms a very dense, tight mat of small, scalloped, blue-green rosettes that closely resemble a miniature echeveria, blushing purple-red at the edges under stress, and produces small white starry flowers on short stalks in summer. Its exceptionally tidy, slow-spreading habit and tolerance of both heat and cold have made it a widely praised rock garden and edging plant, holding its neat form with minimal care. Divide congested mats in spring only if needed, since it spreads slowly and rarely requires renovation.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; low mounding habit suits the front of a border or a rock garden ledge.

directions: Lidakense forms a low, spreading mound of rounded, dusty gray-blue leaves edged and flushed with purple, topped from late summer into fall by dense, dusky-rose flower clusters that age to a deeper wine color and draw butterflies and bees. Its trailing, groundcover-like habit and compact size make it well suited to draping over a wall, edging a path, or filling the front of a border, in contrast to the taller, upright habit of most Hylotelephium cultivars. Grow lean, since rich or overly moist soil produces floppy growth, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
